title: Association Between Global Positioning System-Based Training Load and Injury Risk in Recreational Runners: A Large Prospective Study
authors: Cloosterman KLA, de Vos RJ, Willemsen S, van Oeveren B, Visser E, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, et al.
population: Adult recreational runners in the Netherlands registered for 10-42.195 km events, a cohort within an injury-prevention RCT; GPS data shared; mean age 43.8 y, 72.9% men
findings: 461 runners with 20,425 GPS training sessions; 42.3% reported a new running-related injury (RRI) during follow-up.

ACWR was computed per session from distance, duration or speed; Cox regression gave a positive association with RRI onset for distance (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.00-1.74) and duration (HR 1.39, 95% CI 1.07-1.79).
In analyses adjusted for confounders only the duration-based ACWR remained positively associated with RRI onset (HR 1.33, 95% CI 1.02-1.74).
No significant association between ACWR and RRI onset when runners with an RRI at baseline (15.8%) were excluded.
Authors call the clinical relevance questionable given the small HRs and inconsistent outcomes, which makes the role of general training-load advice in RRI prevention uncertain.
461 participants (72.9% men, mean age 43.8 +/- 12.4 years), 20,425 training sessions; 42.3% reported a new RRI during follow-up.
limitations: Abstract-level verification only; the ACWR window lengths are not in the abstract. Lower CI bounds sit at 1.00-1.02, results are not robust to excluding runners injured at baseline, event-registered Dutch runners (73% men) only, self-reported injury. The RCT is not about progression rules, so this is cohort evidence.
implications: A duration exposure shows an association of similar size to distance in a second GPS cohort, so a session-spike guard can be stated on distance or duration; this is weak support (adjusted HR 1.33) and is not a basis for a new numeric threshold.

Do not give the acute:chronic ratio the weight of a hard rule; the association disappears when runners with baseline injury are excluded. A soft warning at most, and only with the injured-at-baseline caveat.
Supports keeping the existing Frandsen 30-day longest-run guard as the primary session rule and treating any ACWR rule as secondary.
Weak support for limiting abrupt increases in time; keep progression gradual but do not treat a spike ratio as a hard cap on long-run length.
Only the duration-based ratio stayed associated after adjustment, a weak hint in favour of specifying load in minutes.
